newsitem.title: SYRIA: Chirac says EU must co-sponsor Mideast talks.
newsitem.headline: Chirac says EU must co-sponsor Mideast talks.

text.p: French President Jacques Chirac, given a hero's welcome in Syria, declared Middle East peace in danger on Saturday and said Europe must co-sponsor Arab-Israeli negotiations, contributing proposals and not just money.

In a dinner speech in Damascus at the start of a six-day Middle East tour, Chirac told Syrian President Hafez al-Assad: "Today, Mr President, we must work together to get the peace process back on track and let it succeed.
"France and Europe must stand by the parties as sources of friendship and proposals, and not as mere partners for reconstruction. It is time for Europe to co-sponsor this process as well," he said.
Assad supported him, accusing Israel's hardline government of completely undermining the peace process and saying there was no contradiction between a European role and U.S. peace efforts.

Chirac did not once mention the United States, the dominant power in the region. But he said there was a need to improve the framework and method of the U.S.-brokered negotiations, reduced to an ill-tempered crawl by Israel's new hardline government.
"The peace process is in danger," he declared.

More than 20,000 people, including children given half a day off school, turned out to cheer Chirac and Assad at Damascus Airport in a staged display of warmth for a visitor hailed by the Syrian media as "one of the best friends of the Arabs".
Omnipresent security men joined the crowd in strewing rose petals in Chirac's patch in a traditional welcome ceremony, and young girls put a garland of white carnations around his neck.
Flag-waving, chanting Syrians, fired up by a band playing Beethoven's Ode to Joy, lined the route through the city to greet the first French president to visit Syria since 1984.

Backing Syria's terms for resuming talks with Israel, Chirac said peace was "only attainable on the basis of the achievements of the negotiations conducted for the last four years". Israel's new government has called for fresh talks without preconditions, which Syria rejects as a return to square one.

Assad said: "It is regrettable and serious that the process initiated at the (1991) Madrid conference seems to be in deadlock today because of the reversal of the current Israeli government of all the efforts and all the commitments achieved in the last five years."
"The position taken by the Israeli government is one of absolute rejection of all the foundations of peace previously agreed, one of abolishing the peace process totally," he said.

Chirac said the key principle of "land for peace", rejected by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, applied both to the Syrian Golan Heights, occupied by Israel since the 1967 Middle East war, and to Lebanon, where both Israel and Syria have troops.
The United States and Israel have signalled reluctance about any political role for France and the European Union in the peace process, of which the EU is the main paymaster.
U.S. Secretary of State Warren Christopher wrote to his EU counterparts in early October urging them to stay out of the Middle East negotiations, French officials said.

Chirac held a first round of talks with Assad before the dinner and is due to have longer talks and a joint news conference on Sunday. On Monday he goes on to Israel and the Paletinian territories, then to Jordan, Lebanon and Egypt.

Syrian Foreign Minister Farouq al-Shara said an agreement ending a festering dispute over repayment of Syria's 1.3 billion franc ($250 million) debt to France would be signed during Chirac's visit, opening the way for new state-guaranteed French investment in Syria and increased trade.
Acknowledging past differences, notably over Lebanon, Chirac said nothing lasting could be accomplished in the Middle East without Syria, and thus without Assad's assistance.
